datasets.name: RainShift benchmark
datasets.description: Benchmark/dataset (Harder et al., Mila/ECMWF) pairing coarse ESM/reanalysis fields with high-res precipitation targets across Global North and Global South regions, purpose-built to test geographic distribution shift in downscaling models.
datasets.variables: precipitation, geographic region labels

datasets.name: SwissMetNet + IMIS station network
datasets.description: 261 automatic weather stations in Switzerland used to train Wind-Topo/DEVINE-style terrain-aware wind downscaling CNNs (dense network analog to the Alps side of a train-dense/deploy-sparse setup).
datasets.variables: wind speed, wind direction, hourly

datasets.name: Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) lidar SWE maps
datasets.description: Used in the Sierra Nevada (CA, 80-94 maps/period) to Colorado Rockies (12 maps/period) transfer-learning SWE study — closest direct US-mountain-range TL precedent found.

datasets.name: Val d'Aran (Spanish Pyrenees) avalanche/snowpack dataset
datasets.description: Independent weather-station, SNOWPACK-simulation, and avalanche-observation dataset used to test Swiss-trained Random Forest avalanche danger/activity models out-of-domain.

datasets.name: ERA5 reanalysis
datasets.description: Standard global 0.25° reanalysis used to pretrain nearly all weather foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, WIND) that are subsequently fine-tuned regionally.

datasets.name: granite-geospatial-wxc-downscaling checkpoints
datasets.description: IBM/NASA fine-tuned version of the Prithvi WxC foundation model for 6x downscaling of MERRA-2 and ECCC fields; concrete example of foundation-model fine-tuning for regional/local downscaling.

datasets.name: MENA regional weather-regional codebase
datasets.description: Pretrained + LoRA-adapted regional weather forecasting checkpoints for the MENA region, released alongside the PEFT localized-adaptation paper.

models.name: DEVINE / Wind-Topo (CNN)
models.description: Convolutional neural network trained on 261 Swiss stations plus 30m topography to downscale NWP wind fields to decametric scale in the Alps. Terrain-aware CNN architecture; not tested outside Switzerland in the literature found, but architecturally the closest existing analog to a 'Swiss-Alps-trained terrain-weather model.'
models.architecture: CNN, topographic descriptors as auxiliary channels

models.name: Random Forest avalanche danger/activity models (SLF)
models.description: Operational Swiss avalanche forecasting RF classifiers trained on 20 years of Swiss data; tested zero-shot/near-zero-shot in the Spanish Pyrenees with 60-70% agreement — direct evidence of cross-mountain-range transfer performance and its limits.
models.architecture: Random Forest
models.transferable: Moderate — same architecture and features transfer, but accuracy drops and local recalibration is recommended

models.name: Aurora
models.description: Large-scale foundation model of the atmosphere (Microsoft), trained on >1M hours of diverse weather/climate data; used as a backbone for downstream fine-tuning (e.g., WeatherPEFT).
models.architecture: 3D Swin-Transformer-based encoder-decoder

models.name: Prithvi WxC
models.description: IBM/NASA foundation model for weather and climate, designed to be fine-tuned for multiple downstream tasks including downscaling.
models.architecture: Transformer-based foundation model

models.name: GraphCast / Pangu-Weather / FourCastNet
models.description: Global medium-range ML weather forecast models trained on ERA5 (0.25°, 37 levels). Studied for regional fine-tuning (e.g., GraphCast fine-tuned on Canadian Global Deterministic Analysis) and as inputs to further dynamical/statistical downscaling (e.g., WRF downscaling of GraphCast output over India), but none of the papers found fine-tune these specifically for mountain-station-level or terrain-scale prediction.
models.architecture: GNN (GraphCast), Vision Transformer (Pangu-Weather), FNO/AFNO (FourCastNet)

models.name: WeatherPEFT
models.description: Task-adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA-family adapters) applied to weather foundation models (incl. Aurora) for downstream regional/task adaptation with far fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning.
models.architecture: PEFT/LoRA adapters on transformer foundation model

models.name: Global-to-Local regional downscaling framework
models.description: Augments a pretrained global weather foundation-model backbone with lightweight multi-scale prediction heads operating in its latent space; achieves ~100x resolution increase for a target region without retraining the backbone. Closest architectural blueprint for 'pretrain globally/broadly, deploy a lightweight terrain-scale head for a specific mountain range.'
models.architecture: Foundation-model backbone (frozen/lightly tuned) + latent-space multi-scale CNN/transformer heads

models.name: SNOWstorm
models.description: Deep-learning emulator for near-surface winds and drifting snow in glaciated mountain environments, trained on high-resolution (50m) idealized simulations, intended to generalize across mid-to-high-latitude glaciated mountain regions.
models.architecture: DL emulator (CNN-based) of idealized LES simulations

models.name: SpLIIF (Sparse Local Implicit Image Function)
models.description: Implicit neural representation trained on sparse weather stations + topography (Japan) enabling arbitrary-resolution downscaling and evaluated for out-of-distribution accuracy — directly targets the 'train sparse, generalize' setting relevant to a data-sparse mountain deployment.
models.architecture: Implicit neural representation (coordinate-based MLP conditioned on local features)

key_findings.finding: No paper was found that trains a terrain-weather model on Swiss Alps data and deploys/evaluates it in North American mountains for meteorological prediction (temperature/wind/precip). This exact transfer path is a literature gap.
key_findings.source: Absence across 10 targeted searches covering transfer learning, domain adaptation, foundation models, and Alps/Rockies-specific queries
key_findings.detail: The closest real analogs found are (a) Swiss-Alps-trained Random Forest avalanche danger/activity models tested in the Spanish Pyrenees (Bacardit et al., ISSW2024 / Cold Regions Sci. & Tech. 2026), and (b) a Sierra Nevada (CA) -> Rocky Mountains (CO) transfer-learning study for snow water equivalent (El Halabi et al. 2025, JGR ML&C). Both are mountain-to-mountain transfer, but neither is Alps-to-North-America nor a general meteorological downscaling model — one is avalanche danger classification, the other is SWE spatial interpolation.

key_findings.finding: Swiss-trained avalanche forecasting models transfer to a different mountain range (Pyrenees) with only moderate fidelity (~60-70% agreement with local forecaster bulletins for dry-snow danger level; weaker for wet-snow activity), without any retraining — this is the best available quantitative evidence for how well an Alps-trained terrain/snow model performs 'as-is' elsewhere.
key_findings.source: From the Swiss Alps to the Pyrenees: Evaluating the transferability of machine learning models for avalanche forecasting (Cold Regions Science and Technology, 2026); Bacardit et al., ISSW2024 P1.27
key_findings.detail: Models were Random Forest classifiers trained on 20 years of Swiss meteorological/snow-cover/danger-level/avalanche-observation data, then run zero-shot on 3 winter seasons of Val d'Aran (Pyrenees) data with matching input pipelines (SNOWPACK simulations from local AWS). The paper frames this explicitly as the first test of cross-mountain-range transferability of an operational ML system, and notes that geographic/climatic variation (snow climate regime) degrades but does not eliminate skill.

key_findings.finding: Transfer learning between data-rich and data-sparse US mountain ranges (Sierra Nevada -> Colorado Rockies) for snow water equivalent improved R2 from 0.45 to 0.54-0.56 and reduced bias ~30%, using geographic/topographic predictors (elevation, slope, aspect, accumulated precip/temp) hypothesized and confirmed via factor analysis to transfer across ranges.
key_findings.source: Modeling Spatial Distribution of Snow Water Equivalent Using Transfer Learning Across Mountainous Basins, JGR Machine Learning and Computation 2025 (El Halabi, Mital, Dwivedi)
key_findings.detail: 94 (later 80 used) lidar SWE maps from California vs. only 12 from Colorado. A base NN model trained on the data-rich California basins was transferred and fine-tuned on the sparse Colorado data. This is the clearest quantitative demonstration in the literature that train-dense/deploy-sparse transfer learning works for a terrain-driven snow variable using topographic predictors, and is the most directly relevant precedent architecturally (though it's SWE mapping, not weather/downscaling per se, and both ranges are within the US).

key_findings.finding: A dedicated benchmark (RainShift) shows deep-learning precipitation downscaling models (GANs, diffusion) suffer substantial performance drops when applied out-of-distribution across geographic regions (Global North -> Global South), and that simply expanding the training domain is insufficient — explicit domain adaptation (e.g., quantile-mapping-based data alignment for zero-shot; fine-tuning for few-shot) is needed to recover skill.
key_findings.source: Benchmarking the geographic generalization of deep learning models for precipitation downscaling / RainShift (Harder, Schmidt et al., Scientific Reports 2026 / arXiv 2507.04930)
key_findings.detail: This is the most rigorous general treatment of 'train in data-abundant region, evaluate in data-sparse region' for spatial downscaling, and directly proposes and tests zero-shot (quantile mapping) and few-shot (fine-tuning) domain-adaptation strategies as the two mainstream approaches.

key_findings.finding: The dominant 2024-2026 architecture pattern for adapting a broad/global pretrained weather model to a specific region or terrain is NOT full retraining but parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/PEFT) or lightweight latent-space heads bolted onto a frozen foundation-model backbone.
key_findings.source: Efficient Localized Adaptation of Neural Weather Forecasting: A Case Study in the MENA Region (arXiv 2409.07585); Task-Adaptive PEFT for Weather Foundation Models / WeatherPEFT (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2509.22020); From Global to Local: Efficient Regional Weather Downscaling with Global Weather Foundation Model (arXiv 2607.03279); granite-geospatial-wxc-downscaling (fine-tuned Prithvi WxC)
key_findings.detail: MENA paper applies LoRA and variants to a pretrained global neural weather model for regional forecasting, improving accuracy/training-speed/memory efficiency versus full fine-tuning. WeatherPEFT does the same generically across weather foundation models (incl. Aurora-class models). The 'Global to Local' paper augments a frozen pretrained weather foundation-model backbone with lightweight multi-scale prediction heads in latent space, achieving ~2-orders-of-magnitude resolution increase for a target region without backbone retraining and outperforming standard image-super-resolution downscaling baselines — this is arguably the best current architectural template for 'train broad, deploy terrain-scale.'

key_findings.finding: Terrain-aware CNN/GNN downscaling architectures trained on dense station networks in one region (e.g., 261 Swiss stations for Wind-Topo/DEVINE; Japan stations for SpLIIF) explicitly target the sparse-network generalization problem and report meaningful accuracy gains over interpolation baselines, but published evaluation of these specific models has not extended to a different continent's mountain range.
key_findings.source: Wind-Topo/DEVINE (Dujardin & Lehning, QJRMS 2022); Sparse Local Implicit Image Function for sub-km Weather Downscaling (arXiv 2510.20228, NeurIPS 2025 workshop)
key_findings.detail: DEVINE/Wind-Topo is a CNN trained on Swiss IMIS+SwissMetNet stations plus 30m topography to downscale NWP wind to decametric resolution in the Alps — the clearest 'dense Alpine network' training precedent, but the papers found test it only within Switzerland. SpLIIF (implicit neural representation) is trained on sparse Japanese stations+topography and explicitly evaluates in- vs. out-of-distribution accuracy, beating CorrDiff and interpolation baselines by 10-50%, but again within-country, not cross-continent.

result.dimension: Transfer learning and cross-region domain adaptation for mountain meteorology and terrain-scale weather/spatial downscaling — literature survey answering whether models trained in data-rich mountain regions (e.g., Swiss Alps) have been transferred/adapted to data-sparse mountain regions (e.g., North American ranges), and what architectures (foundation models, PEFT, terrain-aware CNNs/GNNs/INRs, domain adaptation) are used to do it.
implications: No literature was found doing the exact 'train on Swiss Alps data, deploy in North American mountains' transfer for general meteorological/terrain-weather prediction — this appears to be a genuine, publishable gap rather than well-trodden ground. A project attempting this would be among the first, though it can draw directly on adjacent precedents (Alps->Pyrenees avalanche transfer; Sierra Nevada->Rockies SWE transfer) for methodology and expected-performance baselines.

The single best quantitative expectation-setter is the Alps->Pyrenees avalanche transfer result: a well-validated Swiss model applied as-is to a different mountain range achieved only ~60-70% agreement with local ground truth — i.e., expect a meaningful accuracy drop from naive zero-shot transfer of a mountain-trained model to a new range, motivating some form of local fine-tuning or domain adaptation rather than pure zero-shot deployment.

The RainShift benchmark's finding — that expanding training-domain diversity alone is insufficient, and that explicit domain adaptation (quantile-mapping data alignment for zero-shot, or light fine-tuning for few-shot) is needed — is directly transferable guidance: any Swiss-Alps-to-Rockies (or similar) system should budget for an explicit adaptation step rather than expecting a purely-global or purely-source-domain model to generalize.

The Sierra Nevada -> Rockies SWE transfer-learning study is the closest architectural and evaluative precedent for a 'train dense, deploy sparse' terrain-weather pipeline using topographic/geographic predictors (elevation, slope, aspect, snowfall) as the transfer-relevant features — it validates the core hypothesis (via factor analysis) that terrain-driven predictors behave similarly enough across mountain ranges for transfer learning to help, and gives a concrete accuracy uplift benchmark (R2 +20%, bias -30%) to compare against.

The current state-of-the-art architectural pattern to build on is NOT training a terrain model from scratch per region, but taking a pretrained global weather foundation model (Aurora, Prithvi WxC, GraphCast-class) and either (a) LoRA/PEFT-adapting it regionally (MENA case study, WeatherPEFT) or (b) attaching lightweight terrain/latent-space downscaling heads to a frozen backbone (Global-to-Local framework, granite-geospatial-wxc-downscaling) — this is a much cheaper and better-evidenced path than full retraining or naive CNN transfer, and directly suggests: pretrain/leverage a foundation model on broad multi-range data (or start from Aurora/Prithvi/GraphCast), then fine-tune a lightweight terrain-aware head using whatever dense-network data (Swiss Alps or otherwise) is available, and validate/adapt on the sparse target range (Rockies) using few-shot fine-tuning per the RainShift protocol.

Terrain-aware architectures already proven on dense Alpine or comparable networks (DEVINE/Wind-Topo's topography-conditioned CNN; SpLIIF's implicit neural representation over sparse stations+topography; GeoGNN's graph neural network with terrain features) are strong architecture candidates to adapt, since their input representations (topographic descriptors, station graphs) are inherently region-agnostic even though the published training/evaluation has stayed within one country — cross-continent evaluation of these specific architectures appears to be open territory.

datasets.name: NREL WIND Toolkit (WTK / WTK-LED)
datasets.description: WRF-model-derived wind resource dataset for the continental US: meteorological conditions (speed, direction, temperature, pressure, boundary layer height) at multiple hub heights for 2.4M+ sites (2007-2013), plus a newer high-resolution WTK-LED CONUS product (2019-2020, finer grid). Accessible via NREL Developer API (CSV) or bulk S3 (nrel-pds-wtk bucket).
datasets.variables: wind speed/direction at multiple hub heights, temperature, pressure, boundary layer height, friction velocity, turbine power output

datasets.name: DEVINE / wind_downscaling_cnn training data (ARPS + AROME simulations, synthetic Gaussian topographies)
datasets.description: Training data used for the DEVINE CNN: high-resolution (30 m) ARPS atmospheric model simulations over idealized/synthetic Gaussian mountain topographies, plus AROME NWP fields and real observations for validation. Purpose-built for wind-driven snow transport applications, i.e., directly avalanche-adjacent.
datasets.density: 30 m resolution 3D wind fields over synthetic terrain + real French Alps stations
datasets.variables: 3D wind field (speed, direction, vertical component), topographic descriptors (slope, aspect, curvature, exposure)

datasets.name: SNOWstorm training data (idealized high-resolution LES/WRF simulations)
datasets.description: 50 m resolution large-eddy simulations (driven by meso-scale WRF) over semi-idealized glaciated mountain terrain, used to train U-Net emulators for near-surface wind, snow mass change, sublimation, and snow transport flux. Model output archived on Zenodo.
datasets.density: 50 m grid spacing, idealized glaciated mountain domains, mid-to-high latitude winter conditions
datasets.variables: near-surface wind, snow mass change rate, sublimation rate, snow transport flux

datasets.name: FuXi-CFD training/inference data (coarse-resolution atmospheric inputs + 30 m terrain)
datasets.description: AI downscaling framework trained to map coarse-resolution atmospheric fields (reanalysis-scale) to 30 m resolution 3D near-surface wind fields using terrain input; pretrained ONNX model published on Hugging Face with inference example.
datasets.density: 30 m horizontal resolution 3D wind field output from coarse-res atmospheric input
datasets.variables: 3D wind field components, terrain elevation/topography as conditioning input

datasets.name: WindNinja input data (USGS DEM + LANDFIRE vegetation/fuel, NDFD/NOMADS weather init)
datasets.description: Not a curated ML dataset but the standard input stack WindNinja consumes: digital elevation model (auto-downloadable, Arc/Info ASCII, GeoTIFF, ERDAS IMAGINE, or FARSITE .lcp), dominant vegetation/roughness class, and optional NWP initialization (NDFD/NOMADS forecast fields) or a domain-average input wind. Useful as a terrain-feature schema even without WindNinja's solver.
datasets.density: user-supplied DEM resolution (commonly 10-30 m via USGS)
datasets.variables: elevation, vegetation/fuel class (roughness proxy), initial/domain-average wind, optional diurnal/stability inputs

models.name: WindNinja (mass-conserving + RANS solvers)
models.description: USDA Forest Service (Missoula Fire Sciences Lab) diagnostic wind model for complex terrain. Two solvers: a fast finite-element mass-conserving (COM) solver, and a full CFD conservation-of-mass/momentum (COM/Momentum) solver using OpenFOAM's simpleFoam with k-epsilon turbulence, terrain-following mesh (blockMesh/snappyHexMesh). Public-domain license (17 USC 105, US govt work), C++ core, official Python bindings (windninjapy on PyPI) and a third-party CLI wrapper (gagreene/WindNinja). Not ML-based and has no pretrained neural weights -- it is a physics solver, run per-scenario on a DEM.
models.architecture: Physics solver (not a neural net): finite-element mass-conservation solver, or finite-volume RANS (OpenFOAM simpleFoam, k-epsilon)
models.transferable: Not directly as a pretrained backbone (it's a numerical solver, no learned weights to transfer). But it IS directly usable as a physics engine or as a label-generator: run WindNinja over avalanche-terrain DEMs to synthesize (terrain -> wind field) training pairs for a neural surrogate, exactly as DEVINE/SNOWstorm/FuXi-CFD did with ARPS/WRF/LES. Its input schema (DEM + vegetation/roughness class + domain-average or NWP-initialized wind) is a proven minimal terrain-feature set worth mirroring.

models.name: WAsP / PyWAsP (Wind Atlas Methodology)
models.description: DTU's commercial wind resource assessment software implementing the Wind Atlas Methodology (Troen & Petersen 1989): generalizes a measured wind climate to a 'featureless flat terrain' reference (removing local terrain/roughness effects), then downscales that generalized climate to any target site using linear flow models over terrain elevation, roughness-change, and obstacle-sheltering maps. PyWAsP (Python wrapper around the same Fortran core) is now available, still requires a commercial WAsP license.
models.architecture: Linearized analytical/perturbation flow model (not CFD, not ML) plus roughness-change and obstacle models
models.transferable: Commercial license required, no open weights, and it's a linear terrain-flow model, not learnable -- low value as a backbone. Conceptually useful for the generalize/downscale wind-climate framing, and its terrain feature set (elevation + roughness/land-cover + displacement height/obstacles) is a well-validated minimal terrain descriptor set.

models.name: DEVINE (Descente d'Echelle de Vent par Intelligence artificielle pour la Nivologie)
models.description: Fully convolutional U-Net that adapts large-scale (NWP) wind fields to 30 m topography in complex mountain terrain. Trained to replicate the ARPS atmospheric model's behavior over synthetic Gaussian topographies, then validated on French Alps stations. Explicitly built for wind-driven snow transport / nivology applications -- essentially the wind-energy-style terrain downscaling literature applied directly to avalanche-relevant snow science. Code and a follow-on 'two-fold' correction+downscaling model (with pretrained release) are on GitHub/Zenodo.
models.architecture: Fully convolutional neural network / U-Net acting on topographic descriptors (slope, aspect, curvature, sx exposure) + upsampled NWP wind field
models.transferable: High -- this is the closest existing analog to what a micro-weather/avalanche model needs: same input class (DEM-derived topographic descriptors + coarse wind), same output class (high-res near-surface wind), same domain (complex mountain terrain), and it was purpose-built with snow redistribution/avalanche hazard as the motivating application. Pretrained weights are published under a tagged Zenodo release, so this could plausibly be fine-tuned or its CNN architecture reused as a backbone.

models.name: SNOWstorm (v1.0)
models.description: Deep-learning emulator (multiple U-Nets) trained on 50 m LES driven by WRF over idealized glaciated mountain terrain. Takes coarse-to-meso atmospheric variables as input and predicts near-surface wind, snow mass change rate, sublimation rate, and snow transport flux -- i.e., it emulates the full wind-driven snow redistribution chain, not just wind. Code/model archived on Zenodo with hyperparameter tables (weight init, optimizer) published in the supplement.
models.architecture: Multiple task-specific U-Nets (windsurf, snow mass change, sublimation, transport flux), SGD-trained, Xavier-uniform init
models.transferable: High for the snow-redistribution/avalanche-loading piece specifically -- goes beyond wind prediction to directly model snow transport and accumulation from wind + terrain, which is closer to an avalanche-relevant target variable than raw wind speed. Trained on idealized/glaciated terrain, so a transfer step to real avalanche-forecast terrain and mid-latitude storm climates would be needed.

models.name: FuXi-CFD
models.description: AI-based downscaling framework that generates 3D near-surface wind fields at 30 m horizontal resolution from coarse-resolution atmospheric (reanalysis-scale) inputs, explicitly targeting the terrain-induced features (slope jets, flow deflection, recirculation) that km-scale AI weather models average out. Pretrained model published on Hugging Face in ONNX format with a runnable inference example; paper in Nature Communications.
models.architecture: Terrain-informed deep learning downscaling model (CFD-emulating), exported to ONNX for inference
models.transferable: High and immediately usable -- an actual pretrained, downloadable (ONNX, runtime-only) model that does exactly 'coarse weather + terrain -> fine-scale wind field.' Framed for wind energy but architecture-and-purpose identical to what a micro-weather backbone needs. ONNX export means no training code/weights for fine-tuning (inference only) unless the authors release more; still usable directly as a feature-generating front end or for distillation.

models.name: Grid-Kernel Neural Network (Sheehan et al. 2022, replacing WAsP linearized flow model)
models.description: Deep neural network (grid-kernel / CNN-style) trained to predict WAsP-style linearized wind resource grids directly from terrain, intended as a fast learned surrogate for WAsP's analytical flow model.
models.architecture: Grid-Kernel / convolutional deep neural network
models.source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jweia.2022.105123 (Journal of Wind Engineering and Industrial Aerodynamics 229:105123)
models.transferable: Medium -- demonstrates the terrain-to-wind-grid ML pattern (learned surrogate for a physics model) that could be replicated for avalanche terrain, but no public code/weights found in this search.

models.name: TA-ViT (Terrain-Aware Vision Transformer), Terrain-aware neural operators, TerraWind
models.description: Family of 2024-2026 transformer/neural-operator architectures for terrain-aware wind downscaling (25 km->1 km, dual-branch patch embedding fusing terrain and atmospheric tokens; also transformer-based neural operators for full 3D mountain wind fields). Represent the current state of the art in architecture design for terrain-conditioned wind fields.
models.architecture: Vision Transformer with dual-branch terrain/atmosphere patch embedding (TA-ViT); transformer-based neural operator (mesh-free, avoids CFD meshing)
models.transferable: Medium -- no public pretrained weights located in this search, but the architectural pattern (fuse terrain tokens/patches with coarse atmospheric input via cross-attention or dual-branch embedding) is directly reusable as a from-scratch design for an avalanche micro-weather model even without transferring weights.

models.name: windpowerlib
models.description: Open-source (MIT) Python library computing wind turbine/farm power output from wind speed time series (power curves, height correction/wind profile extrapolation, wake losses, power-curve smoothing). Not a terrain-wind field model -- it consumes wind speed as input rather than predicting it from terrain.
models.architecture: Deterministic power-curve and log/power-law height-extrapolation calculations (no ML, no terrain solver)
models.transferable: Low for terrain-wind prediction itself -- useful only if the project needs turbine-style height extrapolation (log-law/power-law wind profiles) as a minor utility, not as a terrain backbone.

key_findings.finding: WindNinja is open source (public domain, no copyright per 17 USC 105) with Python bindings, but it is a physics CFD/mass-conserving solver, not a trained neural network -- there are no pretrained weights to reuse. Its value for this project is as a terrain-feature schema (DEM + vegetation/roughness class + initial wind) and as a synthetic-label generator (run it over target DEMs to create terrain->wind training pairs).
key_findings.source: https://github.com/firelab/windninja ; https://research.fs.usda.gov/firelab/products/dataandtools/windninja-overview ; https://doi.org/10.3390/atmos10110672

key_findings.finding: WAsP is proprietary/commercially licensed (DTU), implementing a linearized analytical Wind Atlas Methodology rather than a learnable model; PyWAsP is a Python wrapper around the same licensed Fortran core, so it is not a usable open backbone. Its terrain input schema (elevation + roughness/land-cover + obstacle/displacement height maps) is a well-validated minimal feature set worth mirroring conceptually.
key_findings.source: https://wasp.dtu.dk/software/wasp/wind-atlas-generation/wind-atlas-methodology ; https://docs.wasp.dk/pywasp/latest/user_guide/topography.html

key_findings.finding: The most directly transferable prior work is NOT from wind-energy per se but from mountain-snow/nivology science that reused the same wind-energy-style terrain-CNN downscaling pattern: DEVINE (Le Toumelin et al. 2023, AIES) is a U-Net trained to downscale NWP wind fields to 30 m over complex terrain, explicitly built for wind-driven snow transport, with pretrained weights and code published (GitHub + tagged Zenodo release).
key_findings.source: https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/aies/2/1/AIES-D-22-0034.1.xml ; https://github.com/louisletoumelin/wind_downscaling_cnn ; https://github.com/louisletoumelin/neural_network_and_devine

key_findings.finding: SNOWstorm (Saigger, Goger & Mölg 2026, GMD) goes one step further than a wind-only model: a set of U-Nets trained on 50 m LES that emulate near-surface wind, snow mass change, sublimation, and snow-transport flux together from coarse atmospheric input. This is functionally closer to an avalanche-relevant 'wind loading' target than pure wind speed, with model output and (per the paper) code archived on Zenodo.
key_findings.source: https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/19/6497/2026/ ; https://zenodo.org/records/17580745

key_findings.finding: FuXi-CFD (2026, Nature Communications) is a wind-energy-framed terrain-informed downscaling model with an actual pretrained model published on Hugging Face in ONNX format, mapping coarse-resolution atmospheric fields plus 30 m terrain to fine-scale 3D near-surface wind. It is the clearest example of a directly downloadable pretrained wind-terrain model, though the public release is inference-only (ONNX), not training-ready weights.
key_findings.source: https://huggingface.co/daisy1212/FuXi-CFD-model ; https://arxiv.org/html/2505.12732v1

key_findings.finding: No pretrained model found in this search was trained specifically for wind-energy resource assessment AND released with fine-tunable open weights ready to drop into another domain -- WAsP and the Grid-Kernel NN successor are closed/no-code; the openly-weighted, transferable examples (DEVINE, SNOWstorm, FuXi-CFD) all originate from atmospheric/cryospheric science groups applying wind-energy-style CNN/U-Net terrain-downscaling architectures to snow and mountain-wind problems, not from wind-energy companies themselves.
key_findings.source: cross-referenced across result_1, result_2, result_3, result_7, result_13, result_14

key_findings.finding: A consistent minimal terrain-feature set recurs across WindNinja, WAsP, and all the ML downscaling papers: elevation/DEM, derived slope and aspect, a roughness or vegetation/land-cover proxy, and (for the ML models) sheltering/exposure indices such as Sx (upwind terrain exposure) and curvature -- this is a validated starting feature list for a terrain encoder.
key_findings.source: https://firelab.github.io/windninja/pdf/WindNinja_tutorial1.pdf ; https://docs.wasp.dk/pywasp/latest/user_guide/topography.html ; https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/aies/2/1/AIES-D-22-0034.1.xml

key_findings.finding: Separately from wind-terrain models, there is existing avalanche-forecasting ML transfer-learning literature (transferability from Swiss Alps to Pyrenees; transfer learning for data-deficient regions) confirming that terrain/climate transfer across mountain ranges is an active, recognized challenge in this exact application space -- relevant precedent for evaluating how well a wind-energy- or nivology-trained backbone would generalize to a new avalanche-forecast region.

Wind farm wake/terrain interaction models (RANS/LES CFD, physics-informed neural networks for wakes) are largely about turbine-wake superposition on top of a terrain flow field rather than terrain-only wind prediction, making them lower priority as a backbone for a micro-weather/avalanche model -- the terrain-flow component they build on is usually WAsP-linear or generic RANS/LES, not a novel reusable terrain model.
key_findings.source: https://wes.copernicus.org/articles/11/2695/2026/ ; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167610513001827

implications: Do not try to reuse WindNinja or WAsP as neural pretrained backbones -- neither has learnable weights (WindNinja is a physics CFD/mass-conserving solver, WAsP is a closed-source linear analytical model, PyWAsP still requires a paid license). Their real value is as (a) a proven minimal terrain-feature schema (DEM, slope/aspect, roughness/vegetation class, sheltering/exposure) and (b) WindNinja specifically can be run locally (open source, public domain) to generate synthetic terrain->wind training pairs over target avalanche terrain, the same way DEVINE was trained against ARPS output.

The strongest lead for a literal pretrained backbone is FuXi-CFD on Hugging Face (daisy1212/FuXi-CFD-model, ONNX) -- worth downloading and testing directly as a coarse-weather+terrain -> fine wind-field inference module; confirm license terms and whether ONNX-only limits fine-tuning before committing to it.

The strongest lead for a transferable, retrainable architecture (with actual code and published weights) is DEVINE / wind_downscaling_cnn (Le Toumelin et al.) -- it was purpose-built for wind-driven snow transport in complex mountain terrain, is the closest domain match to avalanche micro-weather, and has a tagged Zenodo release; recommend cloning the repo and evaluating the pretrained weights for fine-tuning on target avalanche-region terrain/wind data.

SNOWstorm is worth a closer look beyond wind alone: because it emulates wind-driven snow mass change, sublimation, and transport flux directly, its output variables may map more directly onto avalanche-relevant quantities (windslab loading, redistribution) than a raw wind-speed backbone would -- investigate whether its U-Net architecture or intermediate wind-field predictions can be adapted even if the idealized/glaciated training domain needs updating for real avalanche-forecast terrain.

NREL's WIND Toolkit is a large, open, immediately-downloadable dataset of modeled wind fields (speed/direction at multiple heights, hourly, CONUS) that could serve as auxiliary training/validation data or a sanity-check baseline for any terrain-wind component, independent of which model architecture is chosen.

None of the wind-energy-specific literature offers a plug-and-play pretrained wind-terrain backbone with open, fine-tunable weights; the actually-transferable pretrained artifacts all come from adjacent nivology/cryosphere research groups who already adapted wind-energy-style terrain-CNN methods to snow -- treat this research thread (DEVINE, SNOWstorm) as higher priority than pure wind-energy sources going forward.

Existing avalanche-forecasting ML transfer-learning studies (Alps-to-Pyrenees transferability, data-deficient-region transfer learning) should be read before committing to any single pretrained wind backbone, since they document how much accuracy degrades when moving a model across mountain ranges with different terrain/climate -- relevant to setting expectations for fine-tuning DEVINE/SNOWstorm/FuXi-CFD on a new region.

result.dimension: Cross-domain applications of terrain-weather physics models
implications: The core technical asset — terrain-informed downscaling of wind, temperature, and precipitation — is a horizontal capability with at least 7 distinct proven-or-emerging paying verticals (aviation turbulence, wind/solar siting, hydropower inflow, agricultural frost, wildfire behavior, defense, drone routing). Avalanche/backcountry forecasting is one vertical among many rather than a uniquely defensible niche, which is good for TAM but means differentiation must come from execution, not exclusivity of physics.

Synthetic CFD-generated terrain training data (DEVINE's 7,279 synthetic topographies, FuXi-CFD's large CFD dataset, WindSeer's synthetic training corpus) is a proven, scalable strategy already used by multiple published models to pretrain terrain-wind networks without dense real-world sensor coverage. This directly de-risks the 'labeled data scarcity' problem for a new model — the model can be pretrained on physics-simulator output (CFD/LES) rather than waiting on real-world station density.

Government/defense demand for exactly this capability is not hypothetical: it has standing programs (Army ARTEMIS, IMETS, historic 'Owning the Weather' USAF initiative) and current SBIR/contract dollars (WindBorne's Navy and AFRL contracts for edge-deployed, deep-learning in-theatre NWP). Defense is a credible, funded early-anchor customer segment, separate from and additive to any civilian avalanche/ski product line.

A general-purpose terrain-weather API business model has real commercial and capital-markets precedent: MetGIS (30m terrain-fused forecasts sold to ski resorts, traffic management, open-pit mines), Meteomatics (B2B API across energy/agriculture/aviation), and WindBorne Systems ($37M Series B at a $250M valuation on AI forecasts that beat government models, per TechCrunch/TheNextWeb reporting) all validate that investors and enterprise buyers will pay for terrain/hyperlocal-accurate weather — though the WindBorne coverage explicitly frames monetization, not forecast accuracy, as the harder unsolved problem.

The hyperlocal/terrain-specific weather API market segment is forecast to grow far faster (13.7% CAGR to $4.35B by 2034, per Growth Market Reports) than the generic weather API market (~5% CAGR to $1.39B by 2032, per Market Publishers) — suggesting the terrain-specificity being proposed here is exactly the axis the market is paying a premium for, not a commodity feature.

Ecosystem modeling and mountain urban-heat-island applications are technically strong physics matches (same terrain-driven microclimate/cold-air-pooling mechanisms) but sit in thinner, mostly grant- or municipally-funded markets (conservation biology, climate-adaptation planning) — valuable for scientific credibility, citations, and potential public-sector contracts, but weaker near-term revenue lines than aviation, energy, agriculture, defense, or drone logistics.

The literature converges on a reusable architecture pattern worth adopting directly: pretrain a terrain-to-microclimate backbone on reanalysis (ERA5/ERA5-Land) plus synthetic CFD terrain data, then attach lightweight, domain-specific fine-tuned heads per vertical (frost Tmin classification, fire-relevant surface wind, clear-air/mountain-wave turbulence indices, wind-resource AEP estimates, UAV-scale volumetric wind) — mirroring IBM's Granite-geospatial-wxc-downscaling (fine-tuned from the Prithvi WxC foundation model) and the DEVINE/FuXi-CFD downscaling-head pattern already validated in peer-reviewed work.

key_findings.finding: Wildfire behavior modeling is dominated by terrain-wind coupling physics nearly identical to avalanche terrain-wind modeling
key_findings.source: RAL/UCAR Coupled Weather-Fire Modeling; MDPI Fire 2026 wind-slope review (150+ studies); WRF-SFIRE Bridger Foothills study (npj Natural Hazards 2025); QUIC-URB/QUIC-Fire terrain-following coordinate extension (OSTI)
key_findings.detail: Wind is described as 'often the dominant driver' of fire spread direction/intensity, and operational tools (QUIC-Fire, WRF-SFIRE, FIRETEC) explicitly had to add terrain-following wind solvers to handle complex terrain — the same wind-over-terrain diagnostic/CFD problem central to avalanche forecasting.

key_findings.finding: Hydropower reservoir inflow forecasting in mountain catchments is an active, well-funded ML application built directly on terrain-aware precipitation/snow modeling
key_findings.source: NHESS 2026 reservoir inflow paper; dam inflow deep learning study (Japan, heavy-snowfall region); HESS 2024 mountainous catchment meteorological-forcing evaluation; multiple LSTM/encoder-decoder reservoir inflow papers
key_findings.detail: Studies combine NWP/ensemble rainfall with ML (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, attention encoder-decoders) and snow-cover satellite data over mountain catchments — the precipitation/snowmelt-over-terrain problem is structurally the same 'terrain-precipitation' need described in the task.

key_findings.finding: Agricultural frost prediction in valleys uses cold-air-pooling/drainage physics that is explicitly the same mechanism as avalanche cold-air and wind-terrain interactions, and is already a commercial/operational product in places
key_findings.source: MDPI Atmosphere 2025 Alpine-valley frost ML downscaling (F1=0.78); MDPI Climate 2025 karst cold-air-pool microclimate modeling; WSU AgWeatherNet daily frost forecast program; USGS cold-air-drainage index dataset
key_findings.detail: Papers explicitly describe katabatic/anabatic winds, thermal inversions, and cold-air pooling as the driving mechanism, use terrain features (sky-view factor, wind exposition index, elevation) as ML predictors, and note traditional NWP is 'often inaccurate at the field-scale in complex terrain' — precisely motivating a terrain-weather model. AgWeatherNet (WSU) already runs this operationally for growers.

key_findings.finding: Aviation turbulence/mountain-wave forecasting is a mature, safety-critical, terrain-forced wind-field problem already operational inside national weather services
key_findings.source: AMS BAMS mountain-wave turbulence algorithm paper; NOAA RAP model mountain-wave hybrid-coordinate improvement (WAF 2019); FAA Advisory Circular 00-57 Hazardous Mountain Winds; NAV CANADA mountain wave reference
key_findings.detail: NTSB data cited: meteorological conditions caused 37% of aviation accidents in one period, with icing/turbulence from mountain waves a leading cause; NOAA has had to specifically re-engineer its operational RAP model's vertical coordinate to fix terrain-induced spurious turbulence forecasts — showing strong institutional demand for better terrain-weather physics.

key_findings.finding: Wind and solar resource assessment in complex terrain is a large, mature commercial industry directly reliant on terrain-flow modeling, though the sub-problem differs in emphasis (steady-state flow/shading vs. transient weather)
key_findings.source: PSE Community complex-terrain wind resource decision-process paper; Wind Energy Science 2022 review of complex-terrain wind energy R&D needs; MDPI Remote Sensing 2026 automated satellite-based wind site assessment; Solargis/RatedPower/LuSim terrain-adapted PV tools
key_findings.detail: The wind sub-vertical (LiDAR/CFD/ML flow modeling over terrain, automated ERA5+DEM-based site assessment) is the closer physics match; solar siting terrain tools focus more on shading/layout geometry than atmospheric physics, so overlap there is partial.

key_findings.finding: Mountain ecosystem/microclimate modeling for species distribution is a well-established, terrain-driven-temperature academic field, but market is mostly research/conservation funding rather than commercial revenue
key_findings.source: Ecography 2018 microclimate SDM review; Global Ecology and Biogeography 2022 cryptic-refugia SDM study; Biogeosciences 2024 10m radiative-transfer microclimate mapping (Switzerland); USDA PNW 'tree's view of the terrain' BISHOP model
key_findings.detail: Multiple groups build 10-50m resolution terrain-driven temperature/microclimate models for biodiversity/refugia prediction; strong scientific validation of the same physics but funded mainly by conservation grants, not enterprise contracts.

key_findings.finding: Urban heat island patterning in mountain cities is measurably distinct from flat-terrain UHI and modeled with the same terrain-circulation physics (katabatic flow, basin cold pools, mountain blockage)
key_findings.source: Bolzano Alpine-valley UHI study (ICAM 2025); Kraków relief/UHI study; Hong Kong coastal-wind/complex-terrain WRF heatwave/building-energy study; Doon Valley (Himalayan basin) WRF urban-topography study
key_findings.detail: These are largely academic/municipal-climate-adaptation studies (WRF-based), suggesting a public-sector/consulting revenue path rather than a direct consumer product, but confirm the physics transfers cleanly.

key_findings.finding: Military terrain-weather assessment is a long-standing, currently-funded application area with active DoD contracts specifically for AI-based, terrain-aware weather at the tactical edge
key_findings.source: US Army ARTEMIS program (fusing weather data with geospatial/terrain content); Army IMETS system (Wikipedia); WindBorne Systems DoD SBIR/AFRL award for 'In-Theatre Numerical Weather Prediction with Deep Learning-Powered Edge Computing'; Navy SBIR award to AERIS LLC for 'ML-Based Downscaling for High-Resolution Atmospheric Forecasting' ($139,999, 2026)
key_findings.detail: This is the strongest direct evidence of an already-funded government market for exactly this product category — small companies are winning real DoD/Navy/AFRL contracts today for ML-based terrain/weather downscaling at the tactical edge.

key_findings.finding: Drone/UAV routing in complex terrain is the closest technical analog to an avalanche terrain-wind model, with a directly comparable published system
key_findings.source: WindSeer (Microsoft Research / Nature Communications, May 2024) — real-time volumetric wind prediction over complex terrain onboard a small UAV, trained on synthetic data; multiple 2025-2026 papers on wind-aware UAV/drone delivery routing (urban and terrain)
key_findings.detail: WindSeer explicitly targets the same problem shape: high-resolution (much finer than standard NWP's multi-km/hourly scale) wind prediction over complex terrain, running on limited compute, trained on synthetic simulation data — essentially a preview of what a terrain-weather foundation model could look like fine-tuned for a device-deployed use case.

key_findings.finding: A general-purpose terrain-weather API business already has commercial precedent and recent large-scale investor validation, though monetization (not forecast quality) is flagged as the harder problem
key_findings.source: MetGIS company materials (Univ. of Vienna spinoff, 30m terrain-fused forecasts, customers include ski resorts and open-pit mines); Meteomatics business model summary; WindBorne Systems $37M Series B / $250M valuation coverage (TheNextWeb, Aug 2026); weather API market sizing reports (growthmarketreports.com, marketpublishers.com)
key_findings.detail: Hyperlocal/alert-focused weather API market projected to grow at 13.7% CAGR to $4.35B by 2034 versus ~5% CAGR to $1.39B by 2032 for the generic weather API market — implying terrain/hyperlocal specificity is where the growth and pricing power concentrate.

key_findings.finding: Multiple peer-reviewed ML architectures already solve 'terrain + coarse weather in, fine-scale wind/temperature out' as a reusable technique, and some have open pretrained weights
key_findings.source: DEVINE (AMS AIES 2022, CNN trained on ARPS CFD over 7,279 synthetic topographies); FuXi-CFD (Nature Communications 2026, 30m 3D wind fields from CFD-trained network); SR-Weather (npj Climate & Atmospheric Science 2026, 0.25° to 1km temperature super-resolution); IBM Granite geospatial-wxc-downscaling (Hugging Face, fine-tuned from Prithvi WxC foundation model, 6x MERRA-2 temp / 8x wind downscaling, weights publicly available)
key_findings.detail: These directly answer the 'which domains have the richest training data to pretrain' question: synthetic CFD-simulated terrain plus global reanalysis (ERA5/MERRA-2) is the emerging standard pretraining substrate, with fine-tuning onto domain-specific targets (temperature, wind, precipitation) as the transfer step.

result.dimension: Physics-informed / physics-constrained ML for terrain-weather interactions (PINNs, conservation-law-constrained models, neural operators, differentiable simulators, hybrid physics-ML for mountain meteorology)
implications: For a terrain-weather project, the highest-leverage physics constraint is mass conservation (continuity / divergence-free wind, applied via loss term or hard architectural constraint) — it is the most consistently used constraint across PINN wind-field reconstruction (Deep Wind, mass-consistent PINNs) and is cheap to compute (a single differential operator) yet directly fixes a failure mode (spurious mass sources/sinks) that is common when models are applied to terrain not seen in training.

Hard/architectural constraints (built into the network output, e.g. via projection or reparameterization) generalize out-of-distribution better than soft loss-penalty constraints: the JMLR 'Hard-Constrained Deep Learning for Climate Downscaling' paper explicitly tests OOD (temporal split) generalization and finds hard constraints hold up better; 'Enforcing Analytic Constraints in Neural Networks' (PRL) shows architectural conservation constraints hold to machine precision without hurting accuracy. This is directly relevant evidence for the hypothesis that physics constraints improve cross-terrain transfer.

Direct evidence physics constraints help generalization specifically to unseen regimes exists in the climate literature, not yet terrain-specific: 'Towards Physically-consistent, Data-driven Models of Convection' (2002.08525) explicitly reports improved generalization to unseen climates from physical rescaling/constraints; 'Climate-Invariant Machine Learning' (2112.08440) frames climate-regime extrapolation as a generalization problem solved by physics-informed input transforms; 'Spatial Generalization Tests for ML Weather Models' (2607.20716) proposes exactly the kind of OOD/spatial-transfer test a terrain-weather project would need. None of these are terrain-transfer papers per se, but the mechanism (physics constraints = regime-invariant priors) transfers directly to the terrain generalization argument.

Do not build a PINN/conservation model from scratch as a first move: there are already several published, terrain-focused, near-directly-reusable architectures — 'Transformer-based neural operators for 3D wind field prediction over complex mountainous terrain' (Nature Communications Physics 2026) and 'FuXi-CFD' (terrain-informed ML for 30m 3D wind reconstruction) both target exactly this problem (fine 3D wind fields over complex terrain from coarse input) and could be studied as architecture references or even baselines.

For sub-grid/turbulence parameterization in complex terrain, the established literature (GMD 2020 Perdigão TKE dissipation study, 'Learning the structure of wind' DRD model, 'Revealing the Drivers of Turbulence Anisotropy' interpretable-ML study) suggests hybrid non-local, anisotropic turbulence closures learned from terrain-resolving observations outperform local-equilibrium schemes (e.g. MYNN) at fine resolution — relevant if the project needs boundary-layer physics rather than just synoptic-scale wind.

Global mass/energy conservation wrappers (Improving AI Weather Prediction Models Using Global Mass and Energy Conservation Schemes, 2025) are explicitly designed as modular add-ons to existing AIWP backbones (i.e., can likely be bolted onto GraphCast/Pangu/FourCastNet-style models rather than requiring a new architecture) — worth evaluating as a low-effort way to add physical consistency to an existing forecasting pipeline before building bespoke terrain physics.

Differentiable dynamical cores (JAX-based JCM, SpeedyWeather.jl, Breeze/Enzyme.jl) are maturing rapidly (multiple 2025-2026 papers) and specifically support gradient-based hybridization of physics and ML, including a paper on learning terrain-following vertical coordinates via automatic differentiation of the dynamical core itself — this is the most direct 'physics simulator + terrain + ML' convergence point found and worth prototyping against if the project has engineering capacity for a differentiable-solver approach rather than pure PINN loss terms.

Pretrained physics-informed/physics-aware foundation weather models exist and are open-weight (Aurora, Prithvi-WxC, WIND, DeepPrim primitive-equation model) — before training anything from scratch, evaluate whether fine-tuning one of these on terrain-dense regional data plus a conservation-law regularizer meets the project's needs faster than a bespoke architecture.

No papers found propose PINNs/conservation constraints specifically for avalanche or general mountain-hazard forecasting beyond precipitation/wind — the orographic-precipitation ML literature is still largely correlational/statistical (CNN downscaling, radar+DEM kernel methods) rather than physics-constrained; a conservation-law-constrained orographic precipitation model appears to be a genuine gap/opportunity, with the NOAA/GFDL 'hybrid physics-machine learning model for orographic precipitation forecasting' being the closest existing work (nudging-based hybrid, not a hard-constrained PINN).

key_findings.finding: Mass conservation is the most common and most tractable physics constraint for terrain-scale wind-field ML, applied either as a soft loss term (PINN-style) or hard architectural constraint, and consistently improves physical plausibility of reconstructed 3D wind fields from sparse/coarse data.
key_findings.source: Deep Wind Method (wes.copernicus.org, 2025); PMC11308984 PINN weather reconstruction; Hard-Constrained Deep Learning for Climate Downscaling (JMLR 24(365))

key_findings.finding: Enforcing conservation laws (mass, energy, moisture) in AI weather prediction models — either via loss-function penalties or architectural constraints (e.g. explicit renormalization layers) — is achievable to near machine precision without degrading forecast skill, and can be added as a modular wrapper to existing AIWP backbones rather than requiring a new architecture.
key_findings.source: Achieving Conservation of Energy in Neural Network Emulators for Climate Modeling (arXiv 1906.06622); Enforcing Analytic Constraints in Neural Networks (Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 098302); Improving AI Weather Prediction Models Using Global Mass and Energy Conservation Schemes (2025, doi 10.1029/2025ms005138)

key_findings.finding: Physical/architectural constraints measurably improve out-of-distribution generalization in climate/weather ML — tested via temporal-split OOD (Hard-Constrained Deep Learning for Climate Downscaling), unseen warmer-climate stress tests (NSF PAR hybrid physics-ML climate coupling study), and explicit 'generalize to unseen climates' claims for physically-rescaled convection emulators (arXiv 2002.08525) — though direct tests of generalization across unseen terrain specifically (rather than unseen climate regime) were not found.
key_findings.source: arXiv 2002.08525; JMLR 24(365) Hard-Constrained Deep Learning for Climate Downscaling; par.nsf.gov/biblio/10521153; arXiv 2607.20716 Spatial Generalization Tests for ML Weather Models

key_findings.finding: Neural operators (FNO, DeepONet, and transformer-based operator variants) are being actively applied at terrain scale: a 2026 Nature Communications Physics paper demonstrates transformer-based neural operators for 3D wind fields over complex mountainous terrain, and FuXi-CFD reconstructs 30 m-resolution 3D near-surface wind (capturing slope jets, flow deflection, recirimport) from coarse atmospheric input plus high-resolution terrain — these are the most terrain-specific, near-production-ready architectures found.
key_findings.source: Nature Communications Physics (s42005-026-02770-w); Nature Communications FuXi-CFD (s41467-026-70562-5); arXiv 2605.25679

key_findings.finding: Differentiable/GPU-capable atmospheric dynamical cores (JAX Circulation Model / JCM v1.1, SpeedyWeather.jl, Breeze with Enzyme.jl/Reactant.jl) are a fast-maturing 2025-2026 research thread enabling gradient-based hybrid physics-ML, including work on differentiating through terrain-following vertical coordinate systems — the clearest technical path to a genuinely physics-constrained, terrain-aware, end-to-end trainable model.
key_findings.source: GMD JCM v1.1 (gmd.copernicus.org/articles/19/6451/2026); SpeedyWeather.jl (egusphere-egu26-1927); Breeze docs (numericalearth.github.io); 'Learning vertical coordinates via automatic differentiation of a dynamical core' (arXiv 2512.17877)

key_findings.finding: Data-driven turbulence/boundary-layer closures trained on terrain-resolving observational networks (e.g. the Perdigão campaign) outperform standard local-equilibrium schemes (Mellor-Yamada-Nakanishi-Niino) for TKE dissipation rate at fine horizontal resolution in complex terrain; nonlocal, anisotropic ML turbulence models (DRD model) and interpretable random-forest studies of turbulence anisotropy drivers are the state of the art for ABL-over-terrain closure.
key_findings.source: GMD 13, 4271 (2020) Perdigão TKE study; arXiv 2107.11046 DRD model; Boundary-Layer Meteorology s10546-025-00946-5 turbulence anisotropy drivers

key_findings.finding: Orographic precipitation ML remains dominated by statistical/correlational approaches (CNN downscaling, radar+DEM kernel/classification methods, ConvLSTM/FNO/GNN hybrids) rather than hard physics-constrained models; the one clear hybrid physics-ML orographic precipitation model found (GFDL/NOAA, Hsieh et al. 2024) uses a nudging-tendency ML correction on top of a physics model rather than embedded conservation laws — this is a comparatively immature subfield relative to global mass/energy conservation work.
key_findings.source: NOAA repository 61903 (Hsieh, Harris, Clark 2024); AIES doi 10.1175/aies-d-25-0066.1 CNN orographic precipitation gradients; MDPI 13/3/98 Colombian Andes hybrid precipitation study

key_findings.finding: Neural subgrid-scale parameterizations for orography-resolving global storm simulations (predicting heating/moistening tendencies from coarse-grained storm-resolving training data) and multiscale-modeling-framework (MMF) ML emulators are mature, with demonstrated long-term stability techniques (adaptive physical constraints, e.g. CondensNet's water-vapor saturation regulation) — directly relevant if the terrain-weather model needs stable long online rollout rather than one-shot prediction.
key_findings.source: NOAA repository 65641 (Neural Network Parameterization of Subgrid-Scale Physics, Realistic Geography); arXiv 2502.13185v2 CondensNet; Nature Communications s41467-020-17142-3 Stable ML parameterization of subgrid processes

key_findings.finding: Multiple open-weight pretrained 'foundation' weather/atmosphere models exist that could serve as transferable backbones for a terrain-weather project: Microsoft Aurora, NASA-IMPACT Prithvi-WxC, and WIND (zero-shot, task-agnostic, self-supervised) — none are marketed as strictly 'physics-informed' in the PINN sense, but DeepPrim (ICLR 2026) is explicitly a physics-driven primitive-equation-learning 3D forecaster with released code, and represents the closest thing to a pretrained physics-informed weather model found.
key_findings.source: github.com/NASA-IMPACT/Prithvi-WxC; github.com/microsoft/aurora; arXiv 2602.03924 WIND; github.com/DAMO-DI-ML/DeepPrim

models.name: PINN wind-field reconstruction (Navier-Stokes regularized)
models.description: Physics-informed neural network that reconstructs dense wind/pressure fields from sparse weather-station data, regularized by Navier-Stokes equations.
models.architecture: MLP-based PINN with PDE residual loss terms from Navier-Stokes
models.transferable: Loss-function formulation transfers to any terrain domain; would need retraining per region/terrain but architecture is domain-general.

models.name: Deep Wind (mass-consistent PINN for 3D wind reconstruction)
models.description: PINN formulation embedding mass conservation and boundary conditions directly into the loss function for meshless 3D wind field reconstruction from incomplete/noisy data, validated on Super Typhoon Kong-Rey.
models.architecture: Mesh-free PINN with hard mass-conservation + boundary-condition loss terms
models.transferable: Formulation is terrain/geometry-agnostic (mesh-free), a strong candidate to adapt directly to mountain terrain wind reconstruction.

models.name: PhyDL-NWP
models.description: Physics-guided deep learning framework integrating physical equations with latent force parameterization; predicts weather variables at arbitrary spatiotemporal coordinates using automatic differentiation for physics terms plus a physics-informed loss.
models.architecture: Neural field / coordinate-based network + automatic differentiation of governing PDEs + physics-informed loss
models.transferable: Coordinate-based formulation is resolution- and grid-independent, making it naturally suited to irregular terrain; presented for downscaling/forecasting generally, not terrain-specific.

models.name: Hard-Constrained super-resolution / downscaling network
models.description: Deep learning climate/weather downscaling architecture with hard (exact) conservation constraints built into the network output (not just loss penalties), tested for OOD (temporal-split) generalization.
models.architecture: CNN-based super-resolution network with a constraint layer enforcing exact conservation (e.g. mass) on outputs
models.transferable: Constraint-layer technique is architecture-agnostic and directly applicable to terrain-aware downscaling; code released alongside the JMLR paper.

models.name: Neural General Circulation Model (NeuralGCM)
models.description: First hybrid GCM combining a physics-based numerical solver for large-scale dynamics with a learned representation for small-scale/subgrid processes, aiming for both forecast skill and long-term climate stability.
models.architecture: Differentiable dynamical core (spectral solver) + learned neural parameterization module, trained end-to-end
models.transferable: Published as a full hybrid GCM (Google/DeepMind); the coupling pattern (differentiable core + learned subgrid module) is directly reusable for a terrain-focused regional variant.

models.name: JAX Circulation Model (JCM v1.1)
models.description: Open-source, differentiable, intermediate-complexity atmospheric GCM built in JAX, designed to support hybrid physics + data-driven model development with full gradient access.
models.architecture: Differentiable general circulation model implemented in JAX (spectral/grid dynamical core with autodiff support)
models.transferable: Open-source and differentiable end-to-end; well suited as a base to insert a learned, terrain-specific subgrid module trained jointly with the dynamical core.

models.name: SpeedyWeather.jl
models.description: Differentiable, GPU-capable general circulation model in Julia, explicitly built to support ML integration natively into the process-based model rather than training ML separately.
models.architecture: Differentiable spectral dynamical core (Julia/GPU), designed for native coupling with neural network components
models.transferable: General circulation model, not terrain-specialized, but its native ML-coupling design is directly applicable to adding a terrain-effects neural module.

models.name: Transformer-based neural operator for 3D wind fields over complex mountainous terrain
models.description: Operator-learning model (transformer backbone) that predicts full 3D wind fields over complex mountainous terrain, aiming to replace costly CFD + mesh generation for renewable-energy and regional-weather applications.
models.architecture: Transformer-based neural operator (discretization-flexible, operates on terrain + coarse flow input)
models.transferable: Purpose-built for cross-terrain wind field prediction; architecture explicitly designed to generalize across different mountainous domains, making it one of the most directly relevant reference models found.

models.name: FuXi-CFD
models.description: ML framework generating detailed 3D near-surface wind fields at 30 m horizontal resolution from coarse-resolution atmospheric inputs plus high-resolution terrain data, capturing terrain-induced features (slope jets, flow deflection, recirculation) normally lost at km-scale.
models.architecture: Terrain-informed deep learning surrogate for high-resolution CFD-like wind downscaling
models.transferable: Explicitly designed to use terrain information as a conditioning input, making it directly transferable in spirit (if not weights) to any complex-terrain wind-downscaling task.

models.name: Microsoft Aurora
models.description: General-purpose open-weight foundation model for Earth system forecasting covering atmospheric variables, tropical cyclones, ocean waves, and atmospheric chemistry.
models.architecture: Large pretrained transformer-based Earth-system foundation model with task-specific fine-tuned heads
models.transferable: Open weights and code; fine-tunable on regional/terrain-dense data, though not physics-constrained by design out of the box.

models.name: NASA-IMPACT Prithvi-WxC
models.description: Open foundation model for weather and climate (2D vision-transformer-style), with zero-shot examples and downstream fine-tuning task repositories.
models.architecture: 2D vision transformer-style foundation model pretrained on large atmospheric reanalysis corpus
models.transferable: Open weights, explicitly designed for downstream fine-tuning; a plausible backbone to fine-tune for a terrain-focused regional task.

models.name: WIND (Weather Inverse Diffusion)
models.description: Self-supervised, task-agnostic pretrained foundation model for atmospheric modeling achieving strong zero-shot performance across diverse downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.
models.architecture: Diffusion-based self-supervised video-style reconstruction model over atmospheric fields
models.transferable: Zero-shot generalization across tasks is its core claim; worth testing directly on terrain-heavy regional forecasting tasks without fine-tuning first.

models.name: DeepPrim
models.description: Physics-driven 3D deep weather forecaster that learns the primitive equations of atmospheric dynamics for short-term global and regional forecasting (ICLR 2026).
models.architecture: 3D deep network structured around learning primitive-equation dynamics (physics-driven architecture, not just loss-penalty PINN)
models.transferable: Closest match to a genuinely 'physics-informed' pretrained-style weather forecaster found; code released, applicable to regional forecasting including terrain-influenced domains.

models.name: Deep rapid distortion (DRD) turbulence model
models.description: Data-driven, nonlocal, anisotropic synthetic turbulence model for the atmospheric boundary layer, formulated as an operator regression problem over nonlocal covariance kernels parameterized partly by a neural network in Fourier space.
models.architecture: Operator-regression model with neural-network-parameterized nonlocal covariance kernels in Fourier space
models.transferable: Designed to capture nonlocal/anisotropic turbulence structure, directly relevant to terrain-influenced ABL where standard local-equilibrium turbulence closures break down.

datasets.name: ERA5 Reanalysis (ECMWF)
datasets.description: Global atmospheric reanalysis at 0.25° (~25-31km) resolution, 37 pressure levels, hourly from 1940-present. The dominant pretraining corpus for GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, Aurora, AIFS, and NeuralGCM.
datasets.density: 0.25° global grid, hourly
datasets.variables: surface + upper-air (temp, wind, humidity, geopotential, precip, etc.)

datasets.name: CMIP6 climate model ensembles
datasets.description: Multi-model climate simulation archive used to pretrain ClimaX (5.625° and 1.40625° checkpoints).
datasets.density: coarse, ~1-6° depending on source model
datasets.variables: climate variables across multiple GCMs

datasets.name: MERRA-2 (NASA)
datasets.description: NASA reanalysis dataset at 0.5°×0.625° resolution used to pretrain Prithvi-WxC. Coarser than ERA5; active research (IBM/NASA, AGU 2025) on adapting Prithvi-WxC from MERRA-2 to finer ERA5 resolution.
datasets.density: 0.5°×0.625° global, hourly
datasets.variables: atmospheric + land surface

datasets.name: HRRR (High-Resolution Rapid Refresh, NOAA)
datasets.description: 3km CONUS-scale operational NWP analysis used to train NVIDIA StormCast — the one open-weight model here actually operating near terrain/mesoscale resolution.
datasets.density: ~3km, hourly, CONUS only
datasets.variables: 99 state variables incl. boundary-layer vertical structure

datasets.name: WeatherBench 2 (Google Research)
datasets.description: Benchmark framework with cloud-optimized ground-truth (ERA5-derived) and baseline forecast data, plus a live leaderboard scoring GraphCast, Pangu, FourCastNet, NeuralGCM, GenCast, HRES, ENS and others under identical protocols.
datasets.density: 0.25°/1.5° global, 6-hourly
datasets.variables: standard WMO verification variables (z500, t850, wind, precip)

result.dimension: Pre-trained weather/climate models with downloadable weights, evaluated for terrain-scale fine-tuning or feature extraction
implications: No global foundation model natively resolves terrain-scale features (sub-10km): all the headline models (GraphCast, Pangu, FourCastNet, Aurora, ClimaX, Prithvi-WxC, AIFS, NeuralGCM, GenCast) are trained at 0.25° (~25-31km) or coarser. Terrain-scale prediction requires pairing one of these as a global/synoptic backbone with a dedicated downscaling stage (CorrDiff, SR-Weather, SpLIIF, FuXi-CFD, AirCast-SR) or fine-tuning directly against station observations, not using the base model alone.

NVIDIA StormCast is the one directly relevant exception: trained on 3km HRRR data with dense boundary-layer vertical resolution, open weights on HuggingFace (nvidia/stormcast-v1-era5-hrrr), Apache-class Earth-2 licensing, and NVIDIA publishes the training recipe (PhysicsNeMo) — making it the most direct candidate for terrain-scale fine-tuning if the target region has (or can be approximated by) HRRR-like coarse boundary conditions.

Licensing splits the field into two usable camps: fully permissive (Apache 2.0 code + CC BY 4.0 weights for ECMWF AIFS; Apache 2.0/NVIDIA Open Model License for FourCastNet3, StormCast, CorrDiff, Atlas; MIT for ClimaX) versus non-commercial-only (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for GraphCast and GenCast weights; Aurora's GitHub license is 'Other' and Microsoft explicitly requires emailing AIWeatherClimate@microsoft.com for commercial use). This matters immediately if Normandy's terrain-weather work has any commercial angle.

Prithvi-WxC is the model most explicitly engineered for exactly this use case — IBM/NASA built it as a foundation model meant to be fine-tuned for downstream tasks (they maintain a separate 'fine-tuning applications' repo), and there's active 2025 research on adapting it from its native MERRA-2 resolution toward ERA5-class resolution, which is a template for further adapting it toward station-level terrain data.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA-style, per arXiv 2509.22020) is emerging as the practical route to adapt these large foundation models (Aurora, Prithvi-WxC are billion-parameter scale) to a regional dataset without full retraining — worth adopting over full fine-tuning given limited station-level data volume.

For a feature-extractor role specifically, two options stand out: (a) FourCastNet's AFNO/ViT blocks are architecturally simple and easy to lift as a reusable spectral-attention encoder independent of NVIDIA's ecosystem; (b) NASA/IBM's Prithvi-EO (the geospatial, non-weather sibling of Prithvi-WxC) is being used in recent literature (arXiv 2608.12271) as a source of sub-grid terrain/land-cover embeddings that condition a downscaling model — i.e., pair Prithvi-EO (terrain/land features) with a weather backbone (GraphCast/AIFS/StormCast) rather than expecting one model to do both.

AIFS from ECMWF deserves particular attention: it's the only model here that is both fully open (CC BY 4.0) AND comes from the agency that also produces the ERA5/HRES ground truth everyone else trains against — lower distribution-shift risk when fine-tuning against real observations, and no non-commercial restriction to navigate.

key_findings.finding: GraphCast weights are downloadable but restricted to non-commercial use
key_findings.source: github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext (formerly graphcast repo)
key_findings.detail: Weights, normalization stats, and example inputs live on a public Google Cloud Bucket (gs://dm_graphcast); 0.25° resolution, 37 pressure levels, trained on ERA5 1979-2017. Code is Apache 2.0 but the weights themselves are licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. GraphCast has been superseded/folded into the 'weathernext' repo as 'WeatherNext Graph.' Official fine-tuning support is thin (open GitHub issues note the repo 'provides prediction and fine-tuning code, without pretraining infra'), but community fine-tuning exists — e.g. Subich (2024, arXiv:2408.14587) fine-tuned GraphCast on the Canadian Global Deterministic Prediction System at the same 0.25°/37-level structure, with training code published separately at github.com/csubich/graphcast.

key_findings.finding: Pangu-Weather weights are open, ONNX-format, and explicitly ingest terrain via constant masks
key_findings.source: github.com/198808xc/Pangu-Weather
key_findings.detail: Four pretrained models (1hr/3hr/6hr/24hr lead time, ~1.1GB each, ONNX) downloadable from Google Drive/Baidu. 0.25° resolution, 3D Earth-Specific Transformer architecture. Notably ships constant_masks/topography.npy, land_mask.npy, soil_type.npy as static inputs — i.e. terrain is a first-class conditioning signal in the architecture already. PyTorch reimplementations with a load_pretrained_weights() API exist (Helmholtz-AI-Energy/pangu_weather), and NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ships a re-implementation, both making fine-tuning tractable. ECMWF runs it operationally via ai-models-panguweather (Apache 2.0 plugin).

key_findings.finding: FourCastNet's AFNO architecture is open-sourced and reusable independent of the weather task
key_findings.source: github.com/NVlabs/FourCastNet, huggingface.co/nvidia/fourcastnet3
key_findings.detail: Original FourCastNet (ViT + Adaptive Fourier Neural Operator attention) has open code and weights. FourCastNet 3 (current gen) uses a Spherical Fourier Neural Operator (SFNO) for probabilistic ensemble forecasting and is Apache 2.0 licensed, 'ready for commercial/non-commercial use.' Weights on HuggingFace at nvidia/fourcastnet1 and nvidia/fourcastnet3. Part of NVIDIA's broader Earth-2 platform (PhysicsNeMo for training, Earth2Studio/NIM for inference), all under the permissive NVIDIA Open Model License.

key_findings.finding: ClimaX has open MIT-licensed weights but only at coarse climate resolution
key_findings.source: github.com/microsoft/ClimaX, huggingface.co/tungnd/climax
key_findings.detail: Two pretrained checkpoints on HuggingFace: 5.625° and 1.40625° resolution, both pretrained on CMIP6 climate simulation data (not ERA5 weather-forecast-grade data). MIT licensed, explicitly built for downstream fine-tuning including 'climate downscaling' as a documented use case, with a flexible variable-agnostic ViT encoder. Native resolution is far too coarse for direct terrain-scale use, but the architecture/training recipe is a clean reference for building a custom fine-tunable foundation model.

key_findings.finding: Aurora has open weights on HuggingFace but a restrictive license for commercial use
key_findings.source: huggingface.co/microsoft/aurora, github.com/microsoft/aurora
key_findings.detail: Multiple checkpoints available (0.25° Pretrained, 0.25° Fine-Tuned, 0.25° 12-Hour Pretrained, plus specialized variants for air pollution/ocean waves) via the microsoft/aurora HF repo, installable via `pip install microsoft-aurora`. The pip package metadata says MIT, but the GitHub repo license is listed as 'Other' and the README states 'email AIWeatherClimate@microsoft.com if interested in using Aurora for commercial applications' — so treat it as research-use-only until cleared. Architecture and checkpoint-loading are designed for loading custom fine-tuned weights from a HF repo path, making it technically easy to fine-tune.

key_findings.finding: GenCast and NeuralGCM diverge sharply in license terms despite similar Google origins
key_findings.source: github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext, github.com/google-research/neuralgcm
key_findings.detail: GenCast (DeepMind's diffusion-based ensemble model, 0.25°) ships code+weights through the same weathernext repo as GraphCast, under the same CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 non-commercial weight license. NeuralGCM (Google Research's hybrid ML+physics GCM), by contrast, is Apache 2.0 code with pretrained checkpoints on Google Cloud Storage (gs://neuralgcm/models/) under CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike, but commercially usable) — meaningfully more permissive. NeuralGCM's hybrid dynamical-core design also makes it less of a clean 'feature extractor' since much of its skill comes from an embedded physics solver, not a pure learned representation.

key_findings.finding: Prithvi-WxC is the foundation model most explicitly designed for exactly this fine-tuning use case
key_findings.source: huggingface.co/ibm-nasa-geospatial/Prithvi-WxC-1.0-2300M, github.com/NASA-IMPACT/Prithvi-WxC
key_findings.detail: 2.3B-parameter transformer foundation model, open (Apache-style open science license), pretrained on 40 years of MERRA-2 (0.5°×0.625° — coarser than ERA5). NASA/IBM maintain a companion 'fine-tuning applications' set of task-specific repos and are actively publishing on adapting it to finer resolution (IBM Research, 'Exploring Prithvi WXC Adaptation from MERRA2 to ERA5,' AGU 2025) — the closest existing precedent for taking one of these foundation models down to a finer target grid. Sibling model Prithvi-EO (geospatial/land-cover, not weather) is separately being used in recent literature as a source of terrain/land-surface embeddings that condition downscaling models rather than as a weather predictor itself.

key_findings.finding: ECMWF's own AIFS models are fully open (CC BY 4.0) and come from the agency producing the reference data
key_findings.source: huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-single-2.0, aifs-ens-2.0
key_findings.detail: AIFS (Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System) is ECMWF's own encoder-processor-decoder operational AI model, with weights on HuggingFace explicitly licensed CC BY 4.0 (fully open, commercially usable, only attribution required). This wasn't in the original 9-item list but is a highly relevant open, unrestricted alternative to GraphCast/GenCast at similar skill and resolution class.

key_findings.finding: NVIDIA StormCast is the only open-weight model here trained at actual terrain/mesoscale (km) resolution
key_findings.source: huggingface.co/nvidia/stormcast-v1-era5-hrrr
